Summary answer
Explainable AI is both a technical and a socio-organizational challenge. Technical methods can make models more interpretable, but core issues—bias, robustness, and trust—arise from data, incentives, deployment context, and human–AI workflows; they are not solved by models alone. Openness about training processes helps: standardized documentation, audits, and governance reduce risks and improve accountability, but disclosures have limits (provider integrity, practitioner vs end‑user comprehension) and can create new hazards (over‑trust, disclosure-driven harms). Making companies less secretive would materially advance XAI, but it is not a silver bullet; a broader stack—data governance, evaluation standards, independent audits, and human‑in‑the‑loop processes—is required.

1) What “explainable AI” is, and why it is not purely a technical problem
Technical foundations and tensions. Explainability and interpretability research offers model‑level tools (e.g., decision trees, feature attribution via SHAP/LIME, surrogate models) and frameworks to align transparency with safety and accountability, but it consistently surfaces trade‑offs: accuracy vs interpretability, evaluation metric inconsistencies, and robustness gaps. <cite id="47a6b618-0">Surveys of XAI emphasize safety and reliability while documenting challenges in balancing interpretability with performance and the lack of consistent evaluation metrics, with critiques of global interpretation methods and calls for robust evaluative frameworks</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-1">Reviews note accuracy–interpretability trade‑offs and difficulty establishing efficacy of XAI methods, while highlighting benefits for human–AI collaboration and credibility</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-2">A contingency‑theory framing argues prior reviews overemphasize technical benefits and under‑explore conflicting effects of explainability across contexts, motivating strategies that manage opposing trade‑offs</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-3">A strategy perspective proposes three complementary levers: simplifying algorithms, appropriate information disclosure, and high‑level collaboration to increase user understanding</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-4">Human‑centered and responsible AI surveys underline that socio‑technical and environmental factors shape AI integration and that explainability sits alongside fairness and accountability within a broader research landscape</cite>.

Socio‑organizational dimensions. Effective explainability requires suitable disclosure and collaborative processes, not just model‑level methods. <cite id="47a6b618-3">Explainability strategies should simplify algorithms, disclose appropriate information, and foster high‑level collaboration to support stakeholder understanding</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-4">Developing and deploying AI involves socio‑cultural and technical factors; preserving human autonomy and control, and understanding deployment impacts, are central challenges for human‑centered AI</cite>.

2) How openness about training processes helps
Artifacts that document data and models. Documentation practices such as Datasheets for Datasets and Model Cards standardize disclosure of data lineage, preprocessing, intended use, performance, and limitations, improving comparability and enabling safer reuse. <cite id="cb7381a7-0">Datasheets aim to create a human‑readable “biography” of datasets so consumers can assess suitability and avoid misuse, while Model Cards provide a standardized reporting framework to compare models on ethical, inclusive, and fair considerations; these have been adopted with tooling (Model Card Toolkit) to integrate into production workflows</cite>. <cite id="cb7381a7-3">Recommended Model Card content includes background on training/evaluation, intended use and non‑uses, and references to dataset sheets; these cards increase transparency but their usefulness hinges on creator integrity</cite>. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Companies widely use model cards and datasheets to describe collection processes, preprocessing, composition, and demographic distributions; however, because providers create these documents, users must trust provider‑stated properties</cite>. <cite id="cb7381a7-0">These documentation practices fit within the wider XAI agenda to make complex systems legible to stakeholders</cite>.

Audits, certification, and governance. Independent and internal audits operationalize accountability, and evidence suggests they can reduce bias and improve trust when integrated into practice. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Transparent practices and documentation (Model Cards, Datasheets) formalize reporting of purpose, assumptions, subgroup performance, and limitations, enabling judgment of fitness for use</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Regulatory frameworks (NIST AI RMF 1.0), standards (ISO/IEC 42001), and governance initiatives institutionalize lifecycle governance, accountability, and transparency, with local laws like NYC Local Law 144 mandating independent third‑party bias audits for employment tools</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Audits—internal or third‑party—are key mechanisms for governance and accountability; public audits have been shown to reduce bias in targeted companies, but many challenges remain across conceptual, technical, economic, and organizational dimensions</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Transparency and audits support accountability, enable bias detection, and facilitate appeals, but blanket mandates to explain can harm welfare when algorithms are fallible; conditional transparency improves outcomes</cite>.

Practitioner‑facing benefits. Openness improves developers’ ability to diagnose failures and align models to organizational constraints. <cite id="6150e93a-0">Transparency about how models decide and what data they were trained on lets developers identify and address bias; providers can enhance transparency via detailed documentation, interpretability tools, and regular audits</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Practitioners employ data‑ and model‑centric exploration (contrast sets, subpopulation analyses) to build understanding; model cards serve organizational alignment and record‑keeping across deployment</cite>.

Limits of openness as a stand‑alone fix
Provider integrity and information gaps. Documentation is only as reliable as the organizations producing it. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Because model cards/datasheets are authored by providers, recipients must trust the information claimed; this creates a dependency on provider honesty and diligence</cite>. <cite id="cb7381a7-3">The usefulness and accuracy of model cards rely on the integrity and completeness of the creator; standardization is unlikely in the near term, making documentation one tool among many</cite>.

Practitioner vs end‑user comprehension. Much of the benefit of openness accrues to technical stakeholders; end‑users often lack the access or expertise to interpret documentation, so additional mediation (audits, certifications, user‑centric interfaces) is required. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Documentation and technical artifacts increase transparency and help auditors/regulators assess fairness/robustness/privacy, but end‑users typically lack access or expertise to use these artifacts for informed judgments, making certification labels and accessible communication valuable</cite>.

Evaluation and governance gaps. Technical openness does not automatically solve evaluation problems or organizational incentives. <cite id="47a6b618-0">Evaluation frameworks remain inconsistent and robustness is hard to guarantee even with interpretability methods</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-1">Determining the efficacy of XAI methods is difficult, and accuracy–interpretability trade‑offs complicate one‑size‑fits‑all solutions</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Documentation improves reporting but effective bias mitigation requires interdisciplinary collaboration with social scientists and affected communities, which organizations may not institutionalize</cite>.

Security, privacy, and IP constraints. Reducing secrecy can help, but maximal disclosure also exposes risks: retraining on leaked data, adversarial attacks, privacy violations, and competitive harm. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Model cards and datasheets summarize training and data properties; however, when providers must be trusted for the information they publish, withholding sensitive data or methods can be necessary to prevent misuse or leakage that could harm privacy or create security vulnerabilities</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-0">Transparency is crucial for bias identification, but providers must balance openness with privacy and security constraints; practical deployment demands mechanisms that respect these limits</cite>.

The transparency paradox. Over‑confidence in explanations can backfire when models are wrong. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Universal transparency mandates can impose welfare costs when algorithms err; conditional transparency based on confidence thresholds and competence‑adaptive explanations improves efficiency and protects users from misleading guidance, while still enabling accountability</cite>.

3) Would XAI be solved if companies were less secretive?
Partly yes—openness is necessary but not sufficient. Evidence shows that reducing secrecy and adopting standardized documentation, audits, and governance can reduce bias and improve accountability. <cite id="cb7381a7-0">Datasheets and Model Cards increase transparency about data and model properties, helping stakeholders select appropriate assets and integrate them safely</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Public (and internal) audits reduce bias and strengthen governance, though challenges remain</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Standards and laws (NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, NYC bias audits) operationalize accountability and transparency across the lifecycle, showing that organizational and regulatory mechanisms materially change practice</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Transparency aids auditing, bias detection, and appeals, but blanket exposure can harm users when models are fallible; thus, openness must be paired with careful design and mediation</cite>.

No—technical limits and socio‑organizational constraints persist. Even with full disclosure, models remain vulnerable to distribution shift, adversarial attacks, and incentive misalignment; stakeholders differ in needs and literacy; and openness can be exploited. <cite id="47a6b618-0">Interpretability methods themselves face robustness and evaluation critiques, and accuracy–interpretability trade‑offs resist complete resolution</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-1">Efficacy of XAI methods is hard to measure and benefits vary by context; technical solutions alone cannot guarantee trustworthy behavior</cite>. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Trusting provider‑reported properties in model/datasheets creates systemic vulnerabilities if providers omit, misstate, or hide critical issues</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Universal explanations can mislead when models are wrong; governance and conditional disclosure outperform blanket transparency</cite>.

4) What would more likely “solve” XAI: an integrated technical–organizational stack
Data and model provenance plus continuous monitoring. <cite id="cb7381a7-0">Datasheets capture data lineage and intended use to prevent unintentional misuse</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-0">Regular audits and documentation are recommended to ensure algorithms don’t produce biased outputs</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Audits should be structured and ongoing and cover robustness, bias, and fairness; certificates of robustness and human‑in‑the‑loop auditing add guarantees and lived protection</cite>.

Independent verification and regulation. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Regulatory frameworks (NIST AI RMF), standards (ISO/IEC 42001), and local audit mandates (NYC Local Law 144) institutionalize accountability and bias testing</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Policy reforms should move from universal explanation mandates to conditional, welfare‑sensitive transparency and require impact evaluations via randomized trials where feasible</cite>.

Human‑centered design and stakeholder inclusion. <cite id="47a6b618-4">Human‑centered AI requires integrating socio‑technical and environmental factors to preserve autonomy and control</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Effective mitigation needs interdisciplinary collaboration with social scientists, legal scholars, ethicists, and affected communities</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Model cards support organizational alignment and record‑keeping, enabling teams to track performance across subpopulations and confidence levels</cite>.

Guardrails around disclosure. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Because openness relies on provider truthfulness and completeness, organizations should gate sensitive data and methods, and attest claims via verifiable credentials or attestations to reduce trust risks</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-0">Transparency must be balanced with privacy, security, and competitiveness; tools and processes should respect these constraints</cite>.

5) Practical roadmap for companies
- Publish data/model cards and datasheets early, and keep them current. <cite id="cb7381a7-0">Datasheets and Model Cards improve reuse safety and comparability; tooling exists to integrate cards into production</cite>. <cite id="cb7381a7-3">Include background, training/eval details, intended use, and quantitative analysis; rely on creator integrity</cite>.
- Implement continuous monitoring and periodic black‑box/white‑box audits. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Audits reduce bias and surface robustness/fairness issues; challenges remain but benefits are documented</cite>.
- Adopt lifecycle governance and align to recognized frameworks. <cite id="6150e93a-1">NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 emphasize accountability, transparency, and lifecycle risk management</cite>.
- Add user‑facing safeguards: conditional explanations and user‑adaptive interfaces. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Conditional transparency and competence‑adaptive explanations improve welfare and protect against misleading guidance</cite>.
- Protect and scope openness: attest claims, red‑team sensitive artifacts, and restrict access to training data. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Openness improves trust, but provider‑stated properties must be verified; sensitive information justifies controlled access</cite>.
- Engage affected communities and cross‑disciplinary teams. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Bias mitigation is more effective with social science, legal, and community input</cite>.

Bottom line
Explainable AI is not “just” a technical problem; it is a cross‑cutting challenge spanning algorithms, data, processes, incentives, and human factors. <cite id="47a6b618-0">Technical methods exist but face accuracy–interpretability trade‑offs and robustness/evaluation gaps</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-1">XAI improves collaboration and accountability but efficacy is hard to measure</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-3">Strategies that combine simpler algorithms, better disclosure, and collaboration increase understanding</cite>. Making companies less secretive would accelerate progress—by enabling documentation, audits, and accountability—but XAI will require governance frameworks, independent verification, and human‑centered design to be truly solved in practice. <cite id="cb7381a7-0">Open documentation practices improve transparency and informed adoption</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Audits and governance reduce bias and strengthen accountability</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Standards and laws institutionalize transparency and risk management</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-4">However, universal transparency can harm when models err; conditional, evidence‑sensitive disclosure and randomized impact evaluation are more effective</cite>.

Open questions and evidence to resolve them
- Causal impact of openness: randomized or quasi‑experimental studies linking increased documentation/audit mandates to measurable reductions in bias/harm across sectors. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Evidence shows public audits reduce bias, but broader causal estimates across contexts remain an open challenge</cite>.
- User‑level outcomes: field experiments on how conditional explanations and user‑adaptive transparency change decisions and appeals, across accuracy regimes. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Conditional transparency improved efficiency and protected users from misleading guidance, motivating wider deployment</cite>.
- Secure openness: empirical measurements of harms from leaked training data or model cards, and effectiveness of verifiable attestations and access controls. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Trusting provider claims creates vulnerabilities; hardware‑assisted attestations and verifiable credentials are proposed to mitigate risks</cite>.

Title: Managing the tension between opposing effects of explainability of artificial intelligence: A contingency theory
Snippet: Research activity and interest in AI, particularly explainability in AI, have grown rapidly in the last few years. The latter authors survey the literature regarding various dimensions and benefits of AI explainability, discuss trends surrounding its sphere, and present key research opportunities in the near term. Similarly, Biran and Cotton (2017) present recent advances on explainability in machine learning models, and Preece (2018) surveys the history of explainability of AI systems as well as its technical challenges, noting that the central challenges of explainability are far from new and arguing that earlier research on explainability of rule-based expert systems offers ideas for making progress toward better understanding of AI today. Guidotti et al. (2018) review black box models and create a taxonomy of interpretability practices and explainability methods in the literature.

All previous reviews focus predominantly on the potential and benefits of explainability of AI and its technical challenges, with less attention to presenting an unbiased and comprehensive view of conflicting effects of explainability in different contexts and for different applications and/or stakeholders. While extant literature on transparency, interpretability and explainability of AI occasionally reports on potential unexpected outcomes of explainability methods and practices, such findings are dispersed, lack detail and are not connected to the bigger picture of the tension between the opposing effects of AI explainability. This gap in reviews to date motivated our attempt to provide a comprehensive examination of the tensions between the opposing effects of AI explainability and the strategies used to manage them.

Title: Providing assurance and scrutability on shared data and machine learning models with verifiable credentials
Snippet: Recent years have seen research attention paid to documentation of ML models and to the data assets that contribute to the models. Gebru et al suggested 'Datasheets for Datasets' 13 , as an attempt to replicate the datasheet format that is common in electrical components for use with shared data assets. The Datasheet's proposal is to produce a human readable story of the data, giving data providers an opportunity to reflect on the nature of the data they are providing, and the ongoing work they need to perform to maintain that data, while providing data users -who will typically be ML model authors -with insights into the data's history and how the data is intended to be used. This relaying of information, almost the biography of the data, is purposeful, in that "transparency on the part of dataset creators is necessary for dataset consumers to be sufficiently well informed that they can select appropriate datasets for their tasks and avoid unintentional misuse". Mitchell, et al., developed this style of documentation further with a proposal for 'Model Cards for Model Reporting' 14 which aims to provide a page or two of information to accompany an ML model, and provides a framework to promote a standardisation of "ethical practice and reporting" to allow practitioners and stakeholders to compare models "along the axes of ethical, inclusive, and fair considerations." 

An intention of Model Cards is to assist less technical users of ML models, and developers who wish to adopt the model as part of a wider system or workflow with insight into how the model should behave and how it can be combined with other models. In summary, Mitchell, et al. argue that researchers sharing ML models should seek to produce Model Cards to aid potential users in becoming better informed on the suitability of particular models for particular use cases. 

Model Cards have been adopted by some organizations since being proposed, and to foster wider adoption, developers have provided an open source tool -the Model Card Toolkit (MCT) 15 -and example documentation on how they can be generated and integrated into a model production workflow. 

Model Cards fit within the wider context of Explainable AI 16 , which seeks to unravel and present the hidden complexities of AI systems to a range of stakeholders, including other developers, and in some cases end-users.

Title: Certification Labels for Trustworthy AI: Insights From an Empirical Mixed-Method Study
Snippet: The question of whether end-users prefer internal or external audits remains to be investigated. 

In addition to defining standards and best practices for AI auditing, it is crucial to consider how the outcomes of audits can be communicated to different stakeholders with varying knowledge and needs [72]. Current research has mainly focused on approaches for documenting machine learning (ML) models and training datasets. These artifacts play an important role in the AI trustworthiness ecosystem by increasing transparency and allowing auditors and regulators to determine whether principles of trustworthy AI (e.g., fairness, robustness, privacy [36]) have been met [37]. For example, "model cards" [14,49] disclose information about a model's purpose and design process, its underlying assumptions, and the model's performance characteristics. Similarly, Gebru et al. introduced "datasheets, " which summarize the motivation, composition, collection process, and recommended uses for datasets, and Floridi et al. recommended the use of "summary datasheets" and "external scorecards. " The former is aligned with the goals of "datasheets" and synthesizes key information about the AI, including its purpose, status, and contact information. The latter is conceptually closely related to "model cards" and evaluates the AI system along several dimensions to form an overall risk score [18]. 

However, these documentations are tailored to AI practitioners, and regulators [37,58,72], rather than end-users affected by AI decisions. Often, end-users have neither the access nor the expertise to understand the technical information that AI documentation provides [1]. It is unlikely that end-users can effectively utilize ML model documentation or data documentation to make informed judgments about trusting or using AI [37]. For this reason, endusers depend on auditors and regulators who can use these artifacts to verify and ensure the trustworthiness of AI. Yet, it remains an open research question of how to effectively communicate to endusers that an audit has considered an AI trustworthy. End-users require accessible communication tailored to their specific values and concerns [72]. A potentially effective way to provide such information is through the use of certification labels, which we will introduce in the following.

Title: When Medical AI Explanations Help and When They Harm
Snippet: Our findings challenge the regulatory consensus embodied in the EU AI Act (European Parliament and Council, 2024), U.S. FDA guidelines, and emerging Chinese frameworks. Current regulations mandate explanations for high-risk AI systems under the assumption that understanding algorithmic reasoning universally improves collaboration. Our evidence demonstrates this assumption is incorrect: universal transparency imposes substantial welfare costs when algorithms are fallible. 

We propose three regulatory reforms. First, move beyond universal mandates to permit conditional transparency based on algorithmic confidence thresholds. Requiring explanations only when AI predictions exceed the 85th percentile of model confidence (conditional accuracy 74.4%) achieves 70% efficiency while protecting users from misleading explanations. Second, enable competence-adaptive systems that adjust explanation provision based on user expertise, achieving 75% efficiency by targeting explanations to lowcompetence users who benefit from correction while protecting high-competence users from misleading advice. Third, require impact evaluation through randomized trials rather than mandating specific transparency mechanisms, given that transparency effects vary systematically with AI accuracy, advice format, and user characteristics. 

The rise of large language models intensifies the transparency paradox. Systems like GPT-4, 5 generate sophisticated explanations maintaining consistent fluency regardless of underlying uncertainty (Bubeck et al., 2023), decoupling explanation quality from recommendation reliability. This amplifies the mechanisms we document: as AI capabilities advance, explanations become more persuasive for both correct and incorrect recommendations, strengthening rather than resolving the paradox. Our theoretical framework, modeling explanations as persuasiveness weights that symmetrically amplify signals, reveals this extends beyond healthcare to any domain with fallible AI assistance, including criminal sentencing (Kleinberg et al., 2018), lending (Fuster et al., 2022), and hiring (Cowgill et al., 2020). While transparency serves important accountability functions-enabling auditing, detecting bias, facilitating appeals-our evidence demonstrates these benefits must be weighed against decision-making harms. Current regulatory approaches sacrifice substantial welfare by prioritizing universal transparency when interpretability and welfare conflict. Contingent transparency frameworks offer a middle path: providing explanations when beneficial while protecting users from misleading guidance when algorithms err, achieving near-optimal welfare while maintaining accountability. 

Our study has limitations suggesting future research directions.

Summary answer
Explainable AI is both a technical and a socio-organizational challenge. Technical methods can make models more interpretable, but core issues—bias, robustness, and trust—arise from data, incentives, deployment context, and human–AI workflows; they are not solved by models alone. Openness about training processes helps: standardized documentation, audits, and governance reduce risks and improve accountability, but disclosures have limits (provider integrity, practitioner vs end‑user comprehension) and can create new hazards (over‑trust, disclosure-driven harms). Making companies less secretive would materially advance XAI, but it is not a silver bullet; a broader stack—data governance, evaluation standards, independent audits, and human‑in‑the‑loop processes—is required.

1) What “explainable AI” is, and why it is not purely a technical problem
Technical foundations and tensions. Explainability and interpretability research offers model‑level tools (e.g., decision trees, feature attribution via SHAP/LIME, surrogate models) and frameworks to align transparency with safety and accountability, but it consistently surfaces trade‑offs: accuracy vs interpretability, evaluation metric inconsistencies, and robustness gaps. <cite id="47a6b618-0">Surveys of XAI emphasize safety and reliability while documenting challenges in balancing interpretability with performance and the lack of consistent evaluation metrics, with critiques of global interpretation methods and calls for robust evaluative frameworks</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-1">Reviews note accuracy–interpretability trade‑offs and difficulty establishing efficacy of XAI methods, while highlighting benefits for human–AI collaboration and credibility</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-2">A contingency‑theory framing argues prior reviews overemphasize technical benefits and under‑explore conflicting effects of explainability across contexts, motivating strategies that manage opposing trade‑offs</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-3">A strategy perspective proposes three complementary levers: simplifying algorithms, appropriate information disclosure, and high‑level collaboration to increase user understanding</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-4">Human‑centered and responsible AI surveys underline that socio‑technical and environmental factors shape AI integration and that explainability sits alongside fairness and accountability within a broader research landscape</cite>.

Socio‑organizational dimensions. Effective explainability requires suitable disclosure and collaborative processes, not just model‑level methods. <cite id="47a6b618-3">Explainability strategies should simplify algorithms, disclose appropriate information, and foster high‑level collaboration to support stakeholder understanding</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-4">Developing and deploying AI involves socio‑cultural and technical factors; preserving human autonomy and control, and understanding deployment impacts, are central challenges for human‑centered AI</cite>.

2) How openness about training processes helps
Artifacts that document data and models. Documentation practices such as Datasheets for Datasets and Model Cards standardize disclosure of data lineage, preprocessing, intended use, performance, and limitations, improving comparability and enabling safer reuse. <cite id="cb7381a7-0">Datasheets aim to create a human‑readable “biography” of datasets so consumers can assess suitability and avoid misuse, while Model Cards provide a standardized reporting framework to compare models on ethical, inclusive, and fair considerations; these have been adopted with tooling (Model Card Toolkit) to integrate into production workflows</cite>. <cite id="cb7381a7-3">Recommended Model Card content includes background on training/evaluation, intended use and non‑uses, and references to dataset sheets; these cards increase transparency but their usefulness hinges on creator integrity</cite>. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Companies widely use model cards and datasheets to describe collection processes, preprocessing, composition, and demographic distributions; however, because providers create these documents, users must trust provider‑stated properties</cite>. <cite id="cb7381a7-0">These documentation practices fit within the wider XAI agenda to make complex systems legible to stakeholders</cite>.

Audits, certification, and governance. Independent and internal audits operationalize accountability, and evidence suggests they can reduce bias and improve trust when integrated into practice. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Transparent practices and documentation (Model Cards, Datasheets) formalize reporting of purpose, assumptions, subgroup performance, and limitations, enabling judgment of fitness for use</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Regulatory frameworks (NIST AI RMF 1.0), standards (ISO/IEC 42001), and governance initiatives institutionalize lifecycle governance, accountability, and transparency, with local laws like NYC Local Law 144 mandating independent third‑party bias audits for employment tools</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Audits—internal or third‑party—are key mechanisms for governance and accountability; public audits have been shown to reduce bias in targeted companies, but many challenges remain across conceptual, technical, economic, and organizational dimensions</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Transparency and audits support accountability, enable bias detection, and facilitate appeals, but blanket mandates to explain can harm welfare when algorithms are fallible; conditional transparency improves outcomes</cite>.

Practitioner‑facing benefits. Openness improves developers’ ability to diagnose failures and align models to organizational constraints. <cite id="6150e93a-0">Transparency about how models decide and what data they were trained on lets developers identify and address bias; providers can enhance transparency via detailed documentation, interpretability tools, and regular audits</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Practitioners employ data‑ and model‑centric exploration (contrast sets, subpopulation analyses) to build understanding; model cards serve organizational alignment and record‑keeping across deployment</cite>.

Limits of openness as a stand‑alone fix
Provider integrity and information gaps. Documentation is only as reliable as the organizations producing it. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Because model cards/datasheets are authored by providers, recipients must trust the information claimed; this creates a dependency on provider honesty and diligence</cite>. <cite id="cb7381a7-3">The usefulness and accuracy of model cards rely on the integrity and completeness of the creator; standardization is unlikely in the near term, making documentation one tool among many</cite>.

Practitioner vs end‑user comprehension. Much of the benefit of openness accrues to technical stakeholders; end‑users often lack the access or expertise to interpret documentation, so additional mediation (audits, certifications, user‑centric interfaces) is required. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Documentation and technical artifacts increase transparency and help auditors/regulators assess fairness/robustness/privacy, but end‑users typically lack access or expertise to use these artifacts for informed judgments, making certification labels and accessible communication valuable</cite>.

Evaluation and governance gaps. Technical openness does not automatically solve evaluation problems or organizational incentives. <cite id="47a6b618-0">Evaluation frameworks remain inconsistent and robustness is hard to guarantee even with interpretability methods</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-1">Determining the efficacy of XAI methods is difficult, and accuracy–interpretability trade‑offs complicate one‑size‑fits‑all solutions</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Documentation improves reporting but effective bias mitigation requires interdisciplinary collaboration with social scientists and affected communities, which organizations may not institutionalize</cite>.

Security, privacy, and IP constraints. Reducing secrecy can help, but maximal disclosure also exposes risks: retraining on leaked data, adversarial attacks, privacy violations, and competitive harm. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Model cards and datasheets summarize training and data properties; however, when providers must be trusted for the information they publish, withholding sensitive data or methods can be necessary to prevent misuse or leakage that could harm privacy or create security vulnerabilities</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-0">Transparency is crucial for bias identification, but providers must balance openness with privacy and security constraints; practical deployment demands mechanisms that respect these limits</cite>.

The transparency paradox. Over‑confidence in explanations can backfire when models are wrong. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Universal transparency mandates can impose welfare costs when algorithms err; conditional transparency based on confidence thresholds and competence‑adaptive explanations improves efficiency and protects users from misleading guidance, while still enabling accountability</cite>.

3) Would XAI be solved if companies were less secretive?
Partly yes—openness is necessary but not sufficient. Evidence shows that reducing secrecy and adopting standardized documentation, audits, and governance can reduce bias and improve accountability. <cite id="cb7381a7-0">Datasheets and Model Cards increase transparency about data and model properties, helping stakeholders select appropriate assets and integrate them safely</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Public (and internal) audits reduce bias and strengthen governance, though challenges remain</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Standards and laws (NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, NYC bias audits) operationalize accountability and transparency across the lifecycle, showing that organizational and regulatory mechanisms materially change practice</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Transparency aids auditing, bias detection, and appeals, but blanket exposure can harm users when models are fallible; thus, openness must be paired with careful design and mediation</cite>.

No—technical limits and socio‑organizational constraints persist. Even with full disclosure, models remain vulnerable to distribution shift, adversarial attacks, and incentive misalignment; stakeholders differ in needs and literacy; and openness can be exploited. <cite id="47a6b618-0">Interpretability methods themselves face robustness and evaluation critiques, and accuracy–interpretability trade‑offs resist complete resolution</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-1">Efficacy of XAI methods is hard to measure and benefits vary by context; technical solutions alone cannot guarantee trustworthy behavior</cite>. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Trusting provider‑reported properties in model/datasheets creates systemic vulnerabilities if providers omit, misstate, or hide critical issues</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Universal explanations can mislead when models are wrong; governance and conditional disclosure outperform blanket transparency</cite>.

4) What would more likely “solve” XAI: an integrated technical–organizational stack
Data and model provenance plus continuous monitoring. <cite id="cb7381a7-0">Datasheets capture data lineage and intended use to prevent unintentional misuse</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-0">Regular audits and documentation are recommended to ensure algorithms don’t produce biased outputs</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Audits should be structured and ongoing and cover robustness, bias, and fairness; certificates of robustness and human‑in‑the‑loop auditing add guarantees and lived protection</cite>.

Independent verification and regulation. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Regulatory frameworks (NIST AI RMF), standards (ISO/IEC 42001), and local audit mandates (NYC Local Law 144) institutionalize accountability and bias testing</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Policy reforms should move from universal explanation mandates to conditional, welfare‑sensitive transparency and require impact evaluations via randomized trials where feasible</cite>.

Human‑centered design and stakeholder inclusion. <cite id="47a6b618-4">Human‑centered AI requires integrating socio‑technical and environmental factors to preserve autonomy and control</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Effective mitigation needs interdisciplinary collaboration with social scientists, legal scholars, ethicists, and affected communities</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Model cards support organizational alignment and record‑keeping, enabling teams to track performance across subpopulations and confidence levels</cite>.

Guardrails around disclosure. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Because openness relies on provider truthfulness and completeness, organizations should gate sensitive data and methods, and attest claims via verifiable credentials or attestations to reduce trust risks</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-0">Transparency must be balanced with privacy, security, and competitiveness; tools and processes should respect these constraints</cite>.

5) Practical roadmap for companies
- Publish data/model cards and datasheets early, and keep them current. <cite id="cb7381a7-0">Datasheets and Model Cards improve reuse safety and comparability; tooling exists to integrate cards into production</cite>. <cite id="cb7381a7-3">Include background, training/eval details, intended use, and quantitative analysis; rely on creator integrity</cite>.
- Implement continuous monitoring and periodic black‑box/white‑box audits. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Audits reduce bias and surface robustness/fairness issues; challenges remain but benefits are documented</cite>.
- Adopt lifecycle governance and align to recognized frameworks. <cite id="6150e93a-1">NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 emphasize accountability, transparency, and lifecycle risk management</cite>.
- Add user‑facing safeguards: conditional explanations and user‑adaptive interfaces. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Conditional transparency and competence‑adaptive explanations improve welfare and protect against misleading guidance</cite>.
- Protect and scope openness: attest claims, red‑team sensitive artifacts, and restrict access to training data. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Openness improves trust, but provider‑stated properties must be verified; sensitive information justifies controlled access</cite>.
- Engage affected communities and cross‑disciplinary teams. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Bias mitigation is more effective with social science, legal, and community input</cite>.

Bottom line
Explainable AI is not “just” a technical problem; it is a cross‑cutting challenge spanning algorithms, data, processes, incentives, and human factors. <cite id="47a6b618-0">Technical methods exist but face accuracy–interpretability trade‑offs and robustness/evaluation gaps</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-1">XAI improves collaboration and accountability but efficacy is hard to measure</cite>. <cite id="47a6b618-3">Strategies that combine simpler algorithms, better disclosure, and collaboration increase understanding</cite>. Making companies less secretive would accelerate progress—by enabling documentation, audits, and accountability—but XAI will require governance frameworks, independent verification, and human‑centered design to be truly solved in practice. <cite id="cb7381a7-0">Open documentation practices improve transparency and informed adoption</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Audits and governance reduce bias and strengthen accountability</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-1">Standards and laws institutionalize transparency and risk management</cite>. <cite id="6150e93a-4">However, universal transparency can harm when models err; conditional, evidence‑sensitive disclosure and randomized impact evaluation are more effective</cite>.

Open questions and evidence to resolve them
- Causal impact of openness: randomized or quasi‑experimental studies linking increased documentation/audit mandates to measurable reductions in bias/harm across sectors. <cite id="6150e93a-2">Evidence shows public audits reduce bias, but broader causal estimates across contexts remain an open challenge</cite>.
- User‑level outcomes: field experiments on how conditional explanations and user‑adaptive transparency change decisions and appeals, across accuracy regimes. <cite id="6150e93a-4">Conditional transparency improved efficiency and protected users from misleading guidance, motivating wider deployment</cite>.
- Secure openness: empirical measurements of harms from leaked training data or model cards, and effectiveness of verifiable attestations and access controls. <cite id="cb7381a7-2">Trusting provider claims creates vulnerabilities; hardware‑assisted attestations and verifiable credentials are proposed to mitigate risks</cite>.
</answer>

Title: A Survey on Interpretability in Visual Recognition
Snippet: Recent surveys on XAI in generic models comprehensively address the classification, applications, and challenges of interpretability techniques. Trustworthy AI principles, particularly safety and reliability, are emphasized by [33] and [34], aligning technical explainability with ethical accountability. Title: Interpreting Black-Box Models: A Review on Explainable Artificial Intelligence
Snippet: A thorough and systematic survey is still lacking despite the large number of surveys that have been conducted to understand the explainability and interpretability of AI. According to researchers, there are currently only a few research papers in this area that give us a brief overview of the best XAI practices. 

An early survey on the matter by Angelov et al. [68] provides an analytical review of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods with a focus on developing AI models that are transparent and interpretable to humans. The authors provide an overview of the current state of XAI, including a review of the various techniques and approaches proposed for achieving explainability in AI models. In addition, they discuss the difficulties and limitations of current approaches, such as the trade-off between accuracy and interpretability and the difficulty of determining the efficacy of XAI methods. The review highlights the potential advantages of XAI for facilitating greater human-AI collaboration and enhancing AI systems' credibility and accountability. 

Guidotti et al. [69] have conducted a comprehensive assessment of approaches for illuminating black-box models that combine machine learning and data mining. They provided a thorough taxonomy that classified the different challenges encountered. Even though the survey was extremely clear about the concepts underlying the idea of explainability, the absence of evaluation as an essential explainability component suggested its inadequacy. Dosilovic et al. [70]. provided a general review of XAI in their paper's closing remarks. They discussed improvements in machine learning models' explainability, paying particular attention to DNNs. This essay demonstrates how human intelligence and artificial general intelligence are interdependent and offers the reader fresh ideas. 

Table 2 summarises the contributions of various works done in the field, along with their strengths and weaknesses. 

A general overview of XAI is provided, along with a detailed breakdown of its contributions, as seen from several angles. While investigating various explicable techniques, we adhere to cognitivism and clarity while exploring different explainable approaches.

Title: Managing the tension between opposing effects of explainability of artificial intelligence: A contingency theory
Snippet: Research activity and interest in AI, particularly explainability in AI, have grown rapidly in the last few years. Many scholars have synthesized the diverse methods and sometimes contradictory findings of survey and review papers in attempts to guide future research in this domain. Some surveys (e.g. Dwivedi et al., 2019;Kaplan and Haenlein, 2019) provide overviews of AI applications and methods, whereas others (e.g. Adadi and Berrada, 2018;Arrieta et al., 2020) provide useful entry points for scholars and practitioners to explore key elements of the young and rapidly growing body of knowledge related to AI transparency and explainability. The latter authors survey the literature regarding various dimensions and benefits of AI explainability, discuss trends surrounding its sphere, and present key research opportunities in the near term. Similarly, Biran and Cotton (2017) present recent advances on explainability in machine learning models, and Preece (2018) surveys the history of explainability of AI systems as well as its technical challenges, noting that the central challenges of explainability are far from new and arguing that earlier research on explainability of rule-based expert systems offers ideas for making progress toward better understanding of AI today. Guidotti et al. (2018) review black box models and create a taxonomy of interpretability practices and explainability methods in the literature.

All previous reviews focus predominantly on the potential and benefits of explainability of AI and its technical challenges, with less attention to presenting an unbiased and comprehensive view of conflicting effects of explainability in different contexts and for different applications and/or stakeholders. While extant literature on transparency, interpretability and explainability of AI occasionally reports on potential unexpected outcomes of explainability methods and practices, such findings are dispersed, lack detail and are not connected to the bigger picture of the tension between the opposing effects of AI explainability. This gap in reviews to date motivated our attempt to provide a comprehensive examination of the tensions between the opposing effects of AI explainability and the strategies used to manage them.

Title: Towards Trustworthy and Understandable AI: Unraveling Explainability Strategies on Simplifying Algorithms, Appropriate Information Disclosure, and High-level Collaboration
Snippet: Such challenges should not only involve overcoming the no-transparency and un-interpretability of black-boxes, but also provide cognitive elements for users and other stakeholders, such as reliability, trust, comprehensibility, and belief. Compared to a large amount of literature on the development and discussion of artificial intelligence (AI) technology and explainable AI (XAI), there is still a significant lack of research aimed at building explainability strategies to help users better understand AI decisions. Therefore, we propose three dimensions for constructing explainability strategies to increase user understanding: simplifying algorithms, appropriate information disclosure, and high-level collaboration.

Title: A Systematic Literature Review of Human-Centered, Ethical, and Responsible AI
Snippet: To situate our review within the broader human-centered, ethical, and responsible AI literature, we next discuss previous surveys that focused on human-centered AI, specific concerns with AI such as fairness and explainability, and surveys dedicated to specific domains of AI. 

Developing AI involves socio-cultural and technical factors, with scholars arguing for developing human-centered AI in the past few years [7,28,67,209]. In particular, there is an emphasis on the challenges of AI integration into socio-technical processes to preserve human autonomy and control, as well as the impacts of AI deployment and applications on society, organizations, and individuals [31,254]. Scholars also argue that understanding socio-technical and environmental factors can surface why and how an AI may become human-centered [65,143,167,208]. 

Despite its recent surge, bias in AI has been a longstanding topic of interest among academic circles [43]. Several surveys discussed data and model biases across domains, including social data biases that stem from user-generated context and behavioral traces [178], gender bias in natural language processing [220], and fairness metrics with potential mitigation strategies [43,179,184]. Others investigated emerging research trends in responsible AI, such as fair adversarial learning, fair word embeddings, fair recommender systems, and fair visual description [184]. 

As AI comes with the promise of advancing our economy and augmenting our lives, it becomes increasingly essential for people to understand AI's implications and remain in control [17]. To this end, much of the previous literature has been dedicated to discussing explainability in AI. For example, a survey of 289 core papers on explanations and explainable systems and more than 12,000 citing papers represents the diverse research landscape of AI, such as algorithmic accountability, interpretable machine learning, context awareness, cognitive psychology, and software learnability [2]. More recently, Angelov et al. [6] provided an overview of AI explainability techniques considering recent advancements in machine learning and deep learning. Methods included featured-oriented ones such as SHapley Additive exPlanation (SHAP) [151], and surrogate models such as Local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) [62].

Many scholars have synthesized the diverse methods and sometimes contradictory findings of survey and review papers in attempts to guide future research in this domain. The latter authors survey the literature regarding various dimensions and benefits of AI explainability, discuss trends surrounding its sphere, and present key research opportunities in the near term. Similarly, Biran and Cotton (2017) present recent advances on explainability in machine learning models, and Preece (2018) surveys the history of explainability of AI systems as well as its technical challenges, noting that the central challenges of explainability are far from new and arguing that earlier research on explainability of rule-based expert systems offers ideas for making progress toward better understanding of AI today. Guidotti et al. (2018) review black box models and create a taxonomy of interpretability practices and explainability methods in the literature.

All previous reviews focus predominantly on the potential and benefits of explainability of AI and its technical challenges, with less attention to presenting an unbiased and comprehensive view of conflicting effects of explainability in different contexts and for different applications and/or stakeholders. While extant literature on transparency, interpretability and explainability of AI occasionally reports on potential unexpected outcomes of explainability methods and practices, such findings are dispersed, lack detail and are not connected to the bigger picture of the tension between the opposing effects of AI explainability. This gap in reviews to date motivated our attempt to provide a comprehensive examination of the tensions between the opposing effects of AI explainability and the strategies used to manage them.

To situate our review within the broader human-centered, ethical, and responsible AI literature, we next discuss previous surveys that focused on human-centered AI, specific concerns with AI such as fairness and explainability, and surveys dedicated to specific domains of AI. 

Developing AI involves socio-cultural and technical factors, with scholars arguing for developing human-centered AI in the past few years [7,28,67,209]. In particular, there is an emphasis on the challenges of AI integration into socio-technical processes to preserve human autonomy and control, as well as the impacts of AI deployment and applications on society, organizations, and individuals [31,254]. Scholars also argue that understanding socio-technical and environmental factors can surface why and how an AI may become human-centered [65,143,167,208]. 

Despite its recent surge, bias in AI has been a longstanding topic of interest among academic circles [43]. Several surveys discussed data and model biases across domains, including social data biases that stem from user-generated context and behavioral traces [178], gender bias in natural language processing [220], and fairness metrics with potential mitigation strategies [43,179,184]. Others investigated emerging research trends in responsible AI, such as fair adversarial learning, fair word embeddings, fair recommender systems, and fair visual description [184]. 

As AI comes with the promise of advancing our economy and augmenting our lives, it becomes increasingly essential for people to understand AI's implications and remain in control [17]. To this end, much of the previous literature has been dedicated to discussing explainability in AI. For example, a survey of 289 core papers on explanations and explainable systems and more than 12,000 citing papers represents the diverse research landscape of AI, such as algorithmic accountability, interpretable machine learning, context awareness, cognitive psychology, and software learnability [2]. More recently, Angelov et al. [6] provided an overview of AI explainability techniques considering recent advancements in machine learning and deep learning. Methods included featured-oriented ones such as SHapley Additive exPlanation (SHAP) [151], and surrogate models such as Local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) [62].

Title: Providing assurance and scrutability on shared data and machine learning models with verifiable credentials
Snippet: Recent years have seen research attention paid to documentation of ML models and to the data assets that contribute to the models. Gebru et al suggested 'Datasheets for Datasets' 13 , as an attempt to replicate the datasheet format that is common in electrical components for use with shared data assets. The Datasheet's proposal is to produce a human readable story of the data, giving data providers an opportunity to reflect on the nature of the data they are providing, and the ongoing work they need to perform to maintain that data, while providing data users -who will typically be ML model authors -with insights into the data's history and how the data is intended to be used. This relaying of information, almost the biography of the data, is purposeful, in that "transparency on the part of dataset creators is necessary for dataset consumers to be sufficiently well informed that they can select appropriate datasets for their tasks and avoid unintentional misuse". Mitchell, et al., developed this style of documentation further with a proposal for 'Model Cards for Model Reporting' 14 which aims to provide a page or two of information to accompany an ML model, and provides a framework to promote a standardisation of "ethical practice and reporting" to allow practitioners and stakeholders to compare models "along the axes of ethical, inclusive, and fair considerations." 

An intention of Model Cards is to assist less technical users of ML models, and developers who wish to adopt the model as part of a wider system or workflow with insight into how the model should behave and how it can be combined with other models. In summary, Mitchell, et al. argue that researchers sharing ML models should seek to produce Model Cards to aid potential users in becoming better informed on the suitability of particular models for particular use cases. 

Model Cards have been adopted by some organizations since being proposed, and to foster wider adoption, developers have provided an open source tool -the Model Card Toolkit (MCT) 15 -and example documentation on how they can be generated and integrated into a model production workflow.

Title: Certification Labels for Trustworthy AI: Insights From an Empirical Mixed-Method Study
Snippet: The question of whether end-users prefer internal or external audits remains to be investigated. 

In addition to defining standards and best practices for AI auditing, it is crucial to consider how the outcomes of audits can be communicated to different stakeholders with varying knowledge and needs [72]. Current research has mainly focused on approaches for documenting machine learning (ML) models and training datasets. These artifacts play an important role in the AI trustworthiness ecosystem by increasing transparency and allowing auditors and regulators to determine whether principles of trustworthy AI (e.g., fairness, robustness, privacy [36]) have been met [37]. Yet, it remains an open research question of how to effectively communicate to endusers that an audit has considered an AI trustworthy. End-users require accessible communication tailored to their specific values and concerns [72]. A potentially effective way to provide such information is through the use of certification labels, which we will introduce in the following.

Summary answer
Explainability is simultaneously about model internals (how a system works), user understanding (why a decision matters to people), and regulatory compliance (what authorities demand to ensure safety and contestability). These framings are not opposites but different audiences for the same underlying question—“what happened, how, and why.” In practice, they can and do conflict: post hoc explanations may not reflect true internals; user-facing rationales can mislead or overload; and compliance templates may not fit users or fail to ensure robust oversight. The strongest designs treat them as a coherent program: document and validate internals, tailor explanations to stakeholder needs, and embed process-based governance that links documentation, user support, and supervisory review across the lifecycle.

1) Three framings of explainability
- Model internals: Technical explainability seeks to make model mechanisms legible—e.g., which features drive predictions, how architectures transform inputs, and dependencies in data pipelines. Practitioners explicitly pursue transparency to “improve understanding of the internal workings of complex models” while building trust with stakeholders, but note that standardizing this and communicating it to non-technical users is hard and confidentiality/sensitivity constrain disclosure, especially in regulated settings <cite id="36032704-0">Ensuring that explainability meets safety and compliance requirements can be challenging, especially in safety-critical applications, with confidentiality and liability concerns; standardized approaches are lacking and clear communication to non-technical users is crucial</cite>. Internally, regulated organizations increasingly treat interpretability/explainability as a trust and transparency pillar within compliance tooling, integrating automated analysis, monitoring, and guidance into governance workflows <cite id="8e3d03cf-1">Interpretability and explainability are prioritized to foster trust and transparency in compliance decisions; NLP enables automated analysis of regulatory texts; predictive analytics forecast compliance risks; continuous monitoring and adaptation are recommended</cite>.

- User understanding: Human-centered explanations aim to improve people’s ability to interpret predictions, calibrate trust, and act appropriately. Empirical HCI studies report that local methods like LIME and SHAP often improve users’ ability to understand predictions, yet effects on trust, satisfaction, and reliance are mixed and context-dependent <cite id="0e5a9041-0">Local explanation methods such as LIME and SHAP can improve users' ability to understand model predictions, but results on trust, satisfaction, and reliance are mixed; visualization attention patterns shape trust; usability and evaluation frameworks (SUS, ESS, TiA) are proposed</cite>. Explanations are tailored by audience: developers, domain experts, and lay users have different needs; user-centered designs improve perceptions of usefulness but not always performance, and early errors can reduce trust for experts while non-experts over-rely on models <cite id="0e5a9041-1">Tailored explanations improve affordability and user satisfaction; early errors decrease trust for domain experts while non-experts over-rely; explanations can improve task performance and trust but sometimes fail or reduce human accuracy and trust due to cognitive and contextual confounders</cite>. Case studies show that people can behave poorly or in biased ways even when shown predictions and explanations, underscoring that explanations alone do not guarantee appropriate reliance <cite id="0e5a9041-2">Users underperformed a risk assessment tool even with predictions and explanations, exhibiting bias-exacerbating behaviors; user-centered design can improve perceived usefulness without performance; trust is shaped by stated and observed accuracy</cite>.

- Regulatory compliance: Compliance framings require evidence, processes, and disclosures that enable oversight, contestability, and risk mitigation. The EU AI Act adopts a risk-based scheme: high-risk systems face transparency, human oversight, and strong documentation obligations; limited-risk systems must inform users; and obligations scale with harm potential <cite id="eba7f7fc-0">The EU AI Act designates high-risk applications with conformity assessments, transparency obligations, and human oversight</cite><cite id="eba7f7fc-1">Risk tiers map to obligations: high-risk systems get the strongest documentation; users need clear instructions; authorities require comprehensive technical documentation</cite>. Although early drafts explicitly referenced interpretability, subsequent versions translated explainability into process and artifact-based requirements such as instructions for use, logs, and access/understanding provisions, including amendments enabling access to algorithms and explanations during compliance investigations <cite id="eba7f7fc-2">The Act’s early draft included interpretability/Article 13 transparency; later revisions replaced direct interpretability mandates with instructions for use, strengthened documentation, log interpretation, and amendments enabling EC access to databases, algorithms, source code, and request explanations during non-compliance</cite>. Sector studies argue regulators should require process-based evidence—traceable design trade-offs, standardized templates for high-risk models, and early legal/compliance involvement—so supervisory focus shifts from whether a model is “explainable” to whether offered explanations are adequate and proportionate to the decisions they support <cite id="36032704-1">Regulators could require documentation of balancing accuracy, compliance, and ease of understanding; process-based obligations (traceable documentation, standardized templates, early legal involvement) shift oversight to adequacy and proportionality of explanations</cite>.

2) How the framings align
- Purpose toward accountability: All three framings converge on making systems accountable—internals for audit, users for safe use, and regulators for oversight. The EU AI Act ties transparency and instructions for use to risk, asking providers to supply accessible information about characteristics, capabilities, and limitations, while also producing comprehensive technical documentation for authorities; this dual audience demands both user-facing clarity and internal traceability <cite id="eba7f7fc-1">High-risk systems must provide clear instructions for users and comprehensive technical documentation for authorities, covering capabilities, limitations, and data used</cite>. Practitioners explicitly note that improving internal understanding supports transparency and trust, and that clear communication to non-technical stakeholders is essential, underscoring a unified goal of accountable deployment <cite id="36032704-0">Transparency and reliability concerns can be addressed through improved understanding of internal workings; building trust with end-users requires effective communication of explainability; standardized approaches and clear requirements are needed</cite>.

- Evidence requirements and artifacts: Compliance frameworks increasingly operationalize explainability in artifacts (data summaries, system logs, instructions for use, access to code/algorithms), which also serve as internal documentation and user guidance. This means “internal” explanations that show feature importance or counterfactuals can be embedded as artifacts and interfaces, aligning technical insight with user comprehension and supervisory review <cite id="eba7f7fc-2">Explainability is realized via instructions for use, strengthened documentation, log interpretation, and amendments enabling access to databases, algorithms, and source code for understanding and compliance checks</cite>. In regulated domains, organizations pair ML-driven monitoring with customer-facing chatbots and guidance, integrating explainability into both risk management and user support <cite id="8e3d03cf-0">AI-driven chatbots provide immediate support and guidance to customers on compliance regulations, enhancing overall compliance; predictive analytics and deep learning improve monitoring and adaptability</cite>.

- Lifecycle integration: Modern governance guidance calls for designing explanations with accuracy, compliance, and ease of understanding simultaneously and involving compliance and business users early so requirements are built in, not bolted on—aligning internal engineering with user-facing UX and audit trails <cite id="36032704-1">Explanation tools must be designed with simultaneous attention to accuracy, compliance, and ease of understanding; compliance and business users should be involved early so explanations are built from the outset</cite>.

3) Where the framings conflict and why
- Post hoc explanations vs. internals: Local post hoc methods (e.g., LIME/SHAP) may highlight spurious or confounded features and not reflect the model’s true decision process, improving perceived understanding yet degrading reliability or even harming downstream decisions; this creates tension between user-facing clarity and faithful disclosure of internals <cite id="0e5a9041-1">Post hoc feature attribution can provide marginal utility and, in some cases, result in worse decisions due to cognitive and contextual confounders</cite>. Practitioners report that revealing internals for trust and compliance is constrained by confidentiality and legal risk, forcing compromises that may understate internal complexity to external audiences <cite id="36032704-0">Confidentiality and liability concerns make it challenging to meet safety, compliance, and stakeholder trust with full internal disclosure; standardized approaches and clear user communication remain unsolved</cite>.

- User understanding vs. safe reliance: Explanations can miscalibrate trust—early errors can reduce expert trust while non-experts over-rely—leading to unsafe behavior despite explanations being “available.” This shows that improving user understanding does not automatically produce appropriate reliance or compliance in practice <cite id="0e5a9041-1">Early errors to domain experts decrease trust; non-experts rely too much on model predictions</cite><cite id="0e5a9041-2">People underperformed a risk assessment tool even with predictions and explanations, exhibiting bias-exacerbating behaviors</cite>. Visualization style affects perceived fairness and justice but there is no universally “best” style, indicating that explanation UX choices can mislead if not grounded in user goals and domain norms <cite id="0e5a9041-1">There is no best approach to explaining algorithmic decisions; user-centered design improves perceived usefulness but not performance</cite>.

- Compliance templates vs. genuine transparency: Regulators often translate explainability into process and artifact requirements (documentation, logs, templates) rather than mandating specific internal architectures. While helpful, these process substitutes may not capture model internals in ways that either users can use or auditors can verify, creating a gap between checkbox compliance and substantive understanding <cite id="eba7f7fc-2">Interpretability provisions evolved into instructions for use, strengthened technical documentation, and access/understanding amendments; these provide indirect but not necessarily substantive internal transparency</cite>. Firms also report that designing for one audience (e.g., customers) may not satisfy supervisors; tailored artifacts and traceable trade-offs are needed for different stakeholders <cite id="eba7f7fc-1">Different stakeholders require different transparency needs: clear instructions for users vs. comprehensive documentation for authorities</cite><cite id="36032704-1">Process-based obligations and stakeholder-specific templates are needed so explanations are adequate and proportionate; early legal involvement aligns explanation requirements with operational needs</cite>.

- Confidentiality/competition vs. oversight: Regulated entities value explainability but face sensitivity and confidentiality constraints; disclosure to supervisors may involve trade-offs, and practitioners highlight risks and liabilities when exposing rationales, especially in financial services and critical infrastructure <cite id="36032704-0">Confidentiality and potential risks/liabilities associated with providing explanations in safety-critical applications make compliance and trust-building challenging</cite><cite id="36032704-1">Regulatory balance requires documenting trade-offs across accuracy, compliance, and understandability; early involvement of legal and compliance teams is critical</cite>.

4) Practical reconciliation: a lifecycle program that unifies internals, users, and compliance
- Define stakeholder-specific “explanation contracts”: Specify what each audience needs and how explanations will be produced, evaluated, and updated. For users: accessible task-relevant rationales; for auditors: traceable data, model summaries, logs, and code access provisions. The EU AI Act’s risk-tailored transparency and documentation provides a template to combine user-facing instructions with comprehensive technical artifacts <cite id="eba7f7fc-1">High-risk systems require clear instructions for users and comprehensive documentation for authorities covering datasets, capabilities, and limitations</cite><cite id="eba7f7fc-2">Strengthened documentation, logs, and access provisions operationalize explainability for oversight</cite>.

- Build from the inside out: Instrument internals for interpretability (log interpretations, model summaries, data governance), then expose them as user-facing guidance and as audit evidence. Practitioner studies emphasize that improving internal understanding supports trust and that standardized internal documentation is necessary; integrating these into user-facing materials reduces ambiguity across audiences <cite id="36032704-0">Improved understanding of internal workings addresses transparency and reliability; standardized explainability approaches and clear requirements are needed</cite><cite id="8e3d03cf-1">Interpretability and explainability foster trust; continuous monitoring and data governance strengthen compliance</cite>.

- Co-design, test, and iterate with users and regulators: Embed UX labs and red-team-style reviews to evaluate whether explanations improve understanding without inducing overreliance or misleading rationales; pair with supervisory playbooks that test adequacy and proportionality. Sector guidance argues for early involvement of legal/compliance and business users so explanations are built in and aligned to operational needs, with process-based documentation of trade-offs <cite id="36032704-1">Early involvement of compliance officers and business users ensures explanations are built from the outset; process-based documentation of trade-offs is recommended</cite><cite id="0e5a9041-0">Usability metrics (SUS, ESS, TiA) systematize evaluation of how explanations influence confidence, understanding, and reliance</cite><cite id="0e5a9041-1">Tailored explanations by audience improve satisfaction; early errors reduce expert trust while non-experts over-rely</cite>.

- Use the right tool for the right audience: Combine model-agnostic post hoc explanations for users with architecture-level diagnostics and counterfactual analyses for review, and with process logs and data lineage for audits. Recognize that post hoc explanations can be useful but can also mislead; add guardrails (e.g., uncertainty, stability checks) and emphasize human-in-the-loop review to mitigate harms <cite id="0e5a9041-1">Local attribution improves understanding but can harm decisions via confounders; guardrails are necessary</cite><cite id="eba7f7fc-2">Instructions for use, logs, and access/understanding provisions serve as indirect measures to ensure traceability and interpretability for compliance</cite>.

5) Takeaways
- Fundamentally, explainability is not one thing; it is a family of commitments—internal transparency, user comprehension, and regulatory accountability—best met with a coherent program that links model internals to user-facing interfaces and supervisory artifacts <cite id="36032704-0">Developing standardized approaches and clear communication to non-technical stakeholders is crucial; transparency and reliability concerns are addressed by improved understanding of internal workings</cite><cite id="eba7f7fc-1">Risk-tailored transparency and comprehensive documentation align user-facing instructions with authority oversight</cite>. 
- The framings can conflict in detail—for instance, when post hoc rationales mislead users or when confidentiality bars full disclosure—but they reinforce each other when governed by process-based requirements, stakeholder-tailored artifacts, and lifecycle integration of evaluation and oversight <cite id="0e5a9041-1">Explanations can fail or reduce human accuracy and trust due to confounders; tailored, audience-specific strategies are needed</cite><cite id="36032704-1">Process-based obligations and early legal/compliance involvement ensure explanations are adequate and proportionate</cite>. 
- Practically, organizations should treat “internal explainability” as engineering evidence, “user explainability” as UX evidence, and “regulatory explainability” as governance evidence, and integrate them via data governance, documentation, evaluation, and continuous monitoring to reduce conflicts and increase trust and compliance <cite id="8e3d03cf-1">Interpretability and explainability foster trust and transparency in compliance; continuous monitoring and adaptation are recommended</cite><cite id="eba7f7fc-1">Strengthened documentation, instructions for use, and data governance practices support compliance and oversight</cite>.
