Summary answer
Explainability is simultaneously about model internals (how a system works), user understanding (why a decision matters to people), and regulatory compliance (what authorities demand to ensure safety and contestability). These framings are not opposites but different audiences for the same underlying question—“what happened, how, and why.” In practice, they can and do conflict: post hoc explanations may not reflect true internals; user-facing rationales can mislead or overload; and compliance templates may not fit users or fail to ensure robust oversight. The strongest designs treat them as a coherent program: document and validate internals, tailor explanations to stakeholder needs, and embed process-based governance that links documentation, user support, and supervisory review across the lifecycle.

1) Three framings of explainability
- Model internals: Technical explainability seeks to make model mechanisms legible—e.g., which features drive predictions, how architectures transform inputs, and dependencies in data pipelines. Practitioners explicitly pursue transparency to “improve understanding of the internal workings of complex models” while building trust with stakeholders, but note that standardizing this and communicating it to non-technical users is hard and confidentiality/sensitivity constrain disclosure, especially in regulated settings <cite id="36032704-0">Ensuring that explainability meets safety and compliance requirements can be challenging, especially in safety-critical applications, with confidentiality and liability concerns; standardized approaches are lacking and clear communication to non-technical users is crucial</cite>. Internally, regulated organizations increasingly treat interpretability/explainability as a trust and transparency pillar within compliance tooling, integrating automated analysis, monitoring, and guidance into governance workflows <cite id="8e3d03cf-1">Interpretability and explainability are prioritized to foster trust and transparency in compliance decisions; NLP enables automated analysis of regulatory texts; predictive analytics forecast compliance risks; continuous monitoring and adaptation are recommended</cite>.

- User understanding: Human-centered explanations aim to improve people’s ability to interpret predictions, calibrate trust, and act appropriately. Empirical HCI studies report that local methods like LIME and SHAP often improve users’ ability to understand predictions, yet effects on trust, satisfaction, and reliance are mixed and context-dependent <cite id="0e5a9041-0">Local explanation methods such as LIME and SHAP can improve users' ability to understand model predictions, but results on trust, satisfaction, and reliance are mixed; visualization attention patterns shape trust; usability and evaluation frameworks (SUS, ESS, TiA) are proposed</cite>. Explanations are tailored by audience: developers, domain experts, and lay users have different needs; user-centered designs improve perceptions of usefulness but not always performance, and early errors can reduce trust for experts while non-experts over-rely on models <cite id="0e5a9041-1">Tailored explanations improve affordability and user satisfaction; early errors decrease trust for domain experts while non-experts over-rely; explanations can improve task performance and trust but sometimes fail or reduce human accuracy and trust due to cognitive and contextual confounders</cite>. Case studies show that people can behave poorly or in biased ways even when shown predictions and explanations, underscoring that explanations alone do not guarantee appropriate reliance <cite id="0e5a9041-2">Users underperformed a risk assessment tool even with predictions and explanations, exhibiting bias-exacerbating behaviors; user-centered design can improve perceived usefulness without performance; trust is shaped by stated and observed accuracy</cite>.

- Regulatory compliance: Compliance framings require evidence, processes, and disclosures that enable oversight, contestability, and risk mitigation. The EU AI Act adopts a risk-based scheme: high-risk systems face transparency, human oversight, and strong documentation obligations; limited-risk systems must inform users; and obligations scale with harm potential <cite id="eba7f7fc-0">The EU AI Act designates high-risk applications with conformity assessments, transparency obligations, and human oversight</cite><cite id="eba7f7fc-1">Risk tiers map to obligations: high-risk systems get the strongest documentation; users need clear instructions; authorities require comprehensive technical documentation</cite>. Although early drafts explicitly referenced interpretability, subsequent versions translated explainability into process and artifact-based requirements such as instructions for use, logs, and access/understanding provisions, including amendments enabling access to algorithms and explanations during compliance investigations <cite id="eba7f7fc-2">The Act’s early draft included interpretability/Article 13 transparency; later revisions replaced direct interpretability mandates with instructions for use, strengthened documentation, log interpretation, and amendments enabling EC access to databases, algorithms, source code, and request explanations during non-compliance</cite>. Sector studies argue regulators should require process-based evidence—traceable design trade-offs, standardized templates for high-risk models, and early legal/compliance involvement—so supervisory focus shifts from whether a model is “explainable” to whether offered explanations are adequate and proportionate to the decisions they support <cite id="36032704-1">Regulators could require documentation of balancing accuracy, compliance, and ease of understanding; process-based obligations (traceable documentation, standardized templates, early legal involvement) shift oversight to adequacy and proportionality of explanations</cite>.

2) How the framings align
- Purpose toward accountability: All three framings converge on making systems accountable—internals for audit, users for safe use, and regulators for oversight. The EU AI Act ties transparency and instructions for use to risk, asking providers to supply accessible information about characteristics, capabilities, and limitations, while also producing comprehensive technical documentation for authorities; this dual audience demands both user-facing clarity and internal traceability <cite id="eba7f7fc-1">High-risk systems must provide clear instructions for users and comprehensive technical documentation for authorities, covering capabilities, limitations, and data used</cite>. Practitioners explicitly note that improving internal understanding supports transparency and trust, and that clear communication to non-technical stakeholders is essential, underscoring a unified goal of accountable deployment <cite id="36032704-0">Transparency and reliability concerns can be addressed through improved understanding of internal workings; building trust with end-users requires effective communication of explainability; standardized approaches and clear requirements are needed</cite>.

- Evidence requirements and artifacts: Compliance frameworks increasingly operationalize explainability in artifacts (data summaries, system logs, instructions for use, access to code/algorithms), which also serve as internal documentation and user guidance. This means “internal” explanations that show feature importance or counterfactuals can be embedded as artifacts and interfaces, aligning technical insight with user comprehension and supervisory review <cite id="eba7f7fc-2">Explainability is realized via instructions for use, strengthened documentation, log interpretation, and amendments enabling access to databases, algorithms, and source code for understanding and compliance checks</cite>. In regulated domains, organizations pair ML-driven monitoring with customer-facing chatbots and guidance, integrating explainability into both risk management and user support <cite id="8e3d03cf-0">AI-driven chatbots provide immediate support and guidance to customers on compliance regulations, enhancing overall compliance; predictive analytics and deep learning improve monitoring and adaptability</cite>.

- Lifecycle integration: Modern governance guidance calls for designing explanations with accuracy, compliance, and ease of understanding simultaneously and involving compliance and business users early so requirements are built in, not bolted on—aligning internal engineering with user-facing UX and audit trails <cite id="36032704-1">Explanation tools must be designed with simultaneous attention to accuracy, compliance, and ease of understanding; compliance and business users should be involved early so explanations are built from the outset</cite>.

3) Where the framings conflict and why
- Post hoc explanations vs. internals: Local post hoc methods (e.g., LIME/SHAP) may highlight spurious or confounded features and not reflect the model’s true decision process, improving perceived understanding yet degrading reliability or even harming downstream decisions; this creates tension between user-facing clarity and faithful disclosure of internals <cite id="0e5a9041-1">Post hoc feature attribution can provide marginal utility and, in some cases, result in worse decisions due to cognitive and contextual confounders</cite>. Practitioners report that revealing internals for trust and compliance is constrained by confidentiality and legal risk, forcing compromises that may understate internal complexity to external audiences <cite id="36032704-0">Confidentiality and liability concerns make it challenging to meet safety, compliance, and stakeholder trust with full internal disclosure; standardized approaches and clear user communication remain unsolved</cite>.

- User understanding vs. safe reliance: Explanations can miscalibrate trust—early errors can reduce expert trust while non-experts over-rely—leading to unsafe behavior despite explanations being “available.” This shows that improving user understanding does not automatically produce appropriate reliance or compliance in practice <cite id="0e5a9041-1">Early errors to domain experts decrease trust; non-experts rely too much on model predictions</cite><cite id="0e5a9041-2">People underperformed a risk assessment tool even with predictions and explanations, exhibiting bias-exacerbating behaviors</cite>. Visualization style affects perceived fairness and justice but there is no universally “best” style, indicating that explanation UX choices can mislead if not grounded in user goals and domain norms <cite id="0e5a9041-1">There is no best approach to explaining algorithmic decisions; user-centered design improves perceived usefulness but not performance</cite>.

- Compliance templates vs. genuine transparency: Regulators often translate explainability into process and artifact requirements (documentation, logs, templates) rather than mandating specific internal architectures. While helpful, these process substitutes may not capture model internals in ways that either users can use or auditors can verify, creating a gap between checkbox compliance and substantive understanding <cite id="eba7f7fc-2">Interpretability provisions evolved into instructions for use, strengthened technical documentation, and access/understanding amendments; these provide indirect but not necessarily substantive internal transparency</cite>. Firms also report that designing for one audience (e.g., customers) may not satisfy supervisors; tailored artifacts and traceable trade-offs are needed for different stakeholders <cite id="eba7f7fc-1">Different stakeholders require different transparency needs: clear instructions for users vs. comprehensive documentation for authorities</cite><cite id="36032704-1">Process-based obligations and stakeholder-specific templates are needed so explanations are adequate and proportionate; early legal involvement aligns explanation requirements with operational needs</cite>.

- Confidentiality/competition vs. oversight: Regulated entities value explainability but face sensitivity and confidentiality constraints; disclosure to supervisors may involve trade-offs, and practitioners highlight risks and liabilities when exposing rationales, especially in financial services and critical infrastructure <cite id="36032704-0">Confidentiality and potential risks/liabilities associated with providing explanations in safety-critical applications make compliance and trust-building challenging</cite><cite id="36032704-1">Regulatory balance requires documenting trade-offs across accuracy, compliance, and understandability; early involvement of legal and compliance teams is critical</cite>.

4) Practical reconciliation: a lifecycle program that unifies internals, users, and compliance
- Define stakeholder-specific “explanation contracts”: Specify what each audience needs and how explanations will be produced, evaluated, and updated. For users: accessible task-relevant rationales; for auditors: traceable data, model summaries, logs, and code access provisions. The EU AI Act’s risk-tailored transparency and documentation provides a template to combine user-facing instructions with comprehensive technical artifacts <cite id="eba7f7fc-1">High-risk systems require clear instructions for users and comprehensive documentation for authorities covering datasets, capabilities, and limitations</cite><cite id="eba7f7fc-2">Strengthened documentation, logs, and access provisions operationalize explainability for oversight</cite>.

- Build from the inside out: Instrument internals for interpretability (log interpretations, model summaries, data governance), then expose them as user-facing guidance and as audit evidence. Practitioner studies emphasize that improving internal understanding supports trust and that standardized internal documentation is necessary; integrating these into user-facing materials reduces ambiguity across audiences <cite id="36032704-0">Improved understanding of internal workings addresses transparency and reliability; standardized explainability approaches and clear requirements are needed</cite><cite id="8e3d03cf-1">Interpretability and explainability foster trust; continuous monitoring and data governance strengthen compliance</cite>.

- Co-design, test, and iterate with users and regulators: Embed UX labs and red-team-style reviews to evaluate whether explanations improve understanding without inducing overreliance or misleading rationales; pair with supervisory playbooks that test adequacy and proportionality. Sector guidance argues for early involvement of legal/compliance and business users so explanations are built in and aligned to operational needs, with process-based documentation of trade-offs <cite id="36032704-1">Early involvement of compliance officers and business users ensures explanations are built from the outset; process-based documentation of trade-offs is recommended</cite><cite id="0e5a9041-0">Usability metrics (SUS, ESS, TiA) systematize evaluation of how explanations influence confidence, understanding, and reliance</cite><cite id="0e5a9041-1">Tailored explanations by audience improve satisfaction; early errors reduce expert trust while non-experts over-rely</cite>.

- Use the right tool for the right audience: Combine model-agnostic post hoc explanations for users with architecture-level diagnostics and counterfactual analyses for review, and with process logs and data lineage for audits. Recognize that post hoc explanations can be useful but can also mislead; add guardrails (e.g., uncertainty, stability checks) and emphasize human-in-the-loop review to mitigate harms <cite id="0e5a9041-1">Local attribution improves understanding but can harm decisions via confounders; guardrails are necessary</cite><cite id="eba7f7fc-2">Instructions for use, logs, and access/understanding provisions serve as indirect measures to ensure traceability and interpretability for compliance</cite>.

5) Takeaways
- Fundamentally, explainability is not one thing; it is a family of commitments—internal transparency, user comprehension, and regulatory accountability—best met with a coherent program that links model internals to user-facing interfaces and supervisory artifacts <cite id="36032704-0">Developing standardized approaches and clear communication to non-technical stakeholders is crucial; transparency and reliability concerns are addressed by improved understanding of internal workings</cite><cite id="eba7f7fc-1">Risk-tailored transparency and comprehensive documentation align user-facing instructions with authority oversight</cite>. 
- The framings can conflict in detail—for instance, when post hoc rationales mislead users or when confidentiality bars full disclosure—but they reinforce each other when governed by process-based requirements, stakeholder-tailored artifacts, and lifecycle integration of evaluation and oversight <cite id="0e5a9041-1">Explanations can fail or reduce human accuracy and trust due to confounders; tailored, audience-specific strategies are needed</cite><cite id="36032704-1">Process-based obligations and early legal/compliance involvement ensure explanations are adequate and proportionate</cite>. 
- Practically, organizations should treat “internal explainability” as engineering evidence, “user explainability” as UX evidence, and “regulatory explainability” as governance evidence, and integrate them via data governance, documentation, evaluation, and continuous monitoring to reduce conflicts and increase trust and compliance <cite id="8e3d03cf-1">Interpretability and explainability foster trust and transparency in compliance; continuous monitoring and adaptation are recommended</cite><cite id="eba7f7fc-1">Strengthened documentation, instructions for use, and data governance practices support compliance and oversight</cite>.

Title: How do ML practitioners perceive explainability? an interview study of practices and challenges
Snippet: Ensuring that explainability meets safety and compliance requirements can be challenging, especially in safety-critical applications. P10 and P12 emphasized ensuring compliance with regulations while providing explainability, addressing concerns about the sensitivity and confidentiality of the algorithm, and dealing with the potential risks and liabilities associated with providing explanations is challenging. 

In conclusion, we observed that developing standardized approaches for explainability and finding effective ways to communicate technical concepts to non-technical users is crucial to overcoming these challenges. Additionally, transparency and reliability concerns can be addressed through an improved understanding of the internal workings of complex models. Building trust with stakeholders and end-users by effectively communicating the explainability of the model is essential. Furthermore, the challenges encountered by ML practitioners in achieving explainability underscore the importance of adopting an RE perspective. Clear and comprehensive communication with non-technical stakeholders is essential, necessitating the identification of user-friendly ways to convey technical concepts. The absence of standardized approaches for explainability calls for the development of clear requirements that guide custom implementations based on specific project needs.

Title: Trade-offs in Financial AI: Explainability in a Trilemma with Accuracy and Compliance
Snippet: This aligns with the recent EU Parliament (2025) resolution on the impact of AI on the financial sector, which highlights the need to balance AI-driven innovation with consumer protection and financial stability, and to avoid overlapping or inconsistent requirements that undermine legal certainty and uptake. Rather than prescribing a single type of explanation, regulators and legislators could require firms to document how they balance accuracy, compliance, and ease of understanding for different stakeholders (e.g., internal risk committees, supervisors, and affected clients), and to justify these choices ex-ante in model governance processes. This points toward process-based obligations (e.g., traceable documentation of trade-offs, standardized explanation templates for high-risk models, and early involvement of legal and compliance teams) so that supervisory dialogue focuses not only on whether a model is "explainable" in the abstract, but on whether the explanations offered are adequate and proportionate to the decisions they support. 

On a practical note, the study suggests that explanation tools must be designed with simultaneous attention to accuracy, compliance, and ease of understanding, rather than optimizing only one dimension, similar to the trustworthiness framework of Fritz-Morgenthal, Hein and Papenbrock (2022), who combine metrics for explainability and fairness as major objectives, with prediction accuracy and speed as secondary benchmarks. The purpose of this is to evaluate the impact of complex models on human lives and businesses, rather than focusing solely on their design or sophistication. Achieving this requires the involvement of compliance officers and business users early in the model lifecycle and not only during validation, so that explanation requirements are built into systems from the outset and aligned with real operational needs.

Title: Explainability as a Compliance Requirement: What Regulated Industries Need from AI Tools for Design Artifact Generation
Snippet: Transforming natural language requirements into design artifacts is a core challenge in RE. Machine Learning (ML) methods have advanced significantly, particularly in domain concept extraction and UML diagram generation [16]- [19], and recent Large Language Model (LLM) studies have shown potential in goal-modeling and UML generation [20]. However, systematic evaluations reveal persistent limitations: these tools struggle with completeness, consistency, and semantic accuracy when processing complex natural language [21]. 

Despite technical progress, there remains a substantial gap between research prototypes and industrial adoption. Reviews indicate that 67-87% of AI tools for RE are confined to lab settings, with merely 7-13% tested in practical contexts [10], [22]. Explainability issues emerge as key barriers, with practitioners valuing transparency as highly as accuracy [23]. Although theoretical frameworks exist for transparency requirements and trace link justifications [24], [25], their validation remains limited to controlled environments rather than real-world contexts where opacity disrupts validation workflows and stakeholder trust [26]. Broader adoption studies identify recurring issues of trust, customization, and integration challenges [27], [28], yet overlook how explainability affects artifact generation, potentially impacting safety. 

Limited industrial case studies provide valuable but partial insights. For instance, explainable classifiers in railway and automotive sectors have shown efficiency and compliance improvements [29]. However, even successful deployments entail extensive manual validation efforts, suggesting hidden inefficiencies [30]. These studies do not explore variations in explainability needs across industries or examine practitioner strategies and associated costs. 

While these industrial studies document technical implementations and outcomes, they overlook a crucial dimension: the practitioner perspective on managing explainability gaps in their daily workflows. Specialized reviews document interpretability limitations across various RE applications including software testing and user stories [31], and traceability [32]. These reviews consistently report shallow practitioner understanding without investigating the underlying causes [33]. Yet no prior work systematically examines how practitioners detect and correct errors when tools provide no justification for their outputs, or investigates the actual strategies teams employ to maintain regulatory compliance when tool reasoning remains opaque. Furthermore, existing studies focus exclusively on active users, missing critical insights from practitioners who have abandoned these tools due to explainability concerns.

Title: Documenting High-Risk AI: A European Regulatory Perspective
Snippet: The obligations defined in the European AI Act are closely linked to defined risk profiles for AI systems, which can be, from highest to lowest: unacceptable risk, covering harmful uses of AI or uses that contravene European Union values and that are consequently prohibited; high risk, covering AI systems that may create an adverse impact on people's safety, health, or fundamental rights under certain circumstances; limited risk, applying to some AI systems that are not considered high risk but whose operation shall be informed to the natural persons exposed to them (for example, chatbots or deepfake videos); and minimal risk, covering all other AI systems that can be deployed in the EU without additional legal obligations beyond those already in place. 

Reasonably, and as depicted in Figure 1, the strongest documentation obligations apply to high-risk AI systems. This is the case for both stakeholder categories considered, which nevertheless have different transparency needs, ranging from clear but concise and accessible instructions of use for users, to comprehensive technical documentation-demonstrating full compliance with the legal requirements-for authorities and conformity assessment bodies. In this context, the question arises whether existing documentation practices-and their wealth of publicly available examples-could be leveraged when formalizing these needs at the technical level in the form of standards. 

To assess this, we have identified, compiled, and classified the main information elements relevant to these stakeholders based on the legal text. These are summarized in Table 1, which also includes for reference the relevant articles where the corresponding information elements are covered. 

The information required encompasses not only the AI systems themselves, but also the datasets used to build them. Indeed, the data used for training, validating, and testing these systems is known to have a substantial impact on their operation, and, if not properly managed, can be a major source of failures and incidents. Accordingly, the data-related elements listed should not only be documented but also be part of a suitable data governance practice.

Title: Explainability in AI Policies: A Critical Review of Communications, Reports, Regulations, and Standards in the EU, US, and UK
Snippet: The path inaugurated by the HLEG and the White Paper informed EC's committees and their intense work on reinforcing the EU AI Act draft [120] proposed in April 2021. The Act adopts a proportional risk-based approach to regulating AI systems, dividing them into three categories of risk with corresponding limitations, transparency requirements, and oversight mechanisms. 

Alongside definitions of risks assessments, transparency, and human oversight, the approach develops a taxonomy of AI actors within data quality requirements and technical documentation. The original draft included provisions for interpretability, specifically Article 13, requiring a sufficient degree of transparency mechanisms for high-risk systems and the attachment of instructions for use containing relevant, accessible, and understandable information to users regarding the characteristics, capabilities, and limitations of performance of these systems. The Act has undergone several revisions as a result of the EC work, prior to inter-institutional negotiations being held in 2023. In April 2022, the IMCO-LIBE committee proposed initial changes to the regulations 2 surrounding AI explainability during inspections [101]. In September 2022, the JURI committee stressed significantly explainability mentions with an Opinion [102] addressing risk mitigation, user interaction and rights 3 . Yet, those revisions were not substantiated in the final draft as presented by the Permanent Representatives Committee on November 25, 2022 [122], including several revisions aimed at ensuring the traceability and interpretability of high-risk AI systems. Title: Explaining AI Without Code: A User Study on Explainable AI
Snippet: Building on this foundation, several empirical studies have investigated how humans interact with explanations of machine learning systems [Narayanan et al., 2018]. Early work has shown that local explanation methods such as LIME [Ribeiro et al., 2016] and SHAP [Sundararajan and Najmi, 2020] can improve users' ability to understand model predictions [Sathyan et al., 2022, Ma et al., 2023, Chiesa-Estomba et al., 2023]. Subsequent research examined how explanation quality impacts user trust, satisfaction, and reliance on automated decisions, but results remain mixed [Papenmeier et al., 2022, Pareek et al., 2024, Westphal et al., 2023]. More recent studies have highlighted the role of visualization in shaping interpretability and trust, particularly through attention-based methods in text classification and medical contexts [Parra et al., 2019, Carvallo et al., 2025]. Meanwhile, tools like Tsundoku demonstrate how explainability can be embedded into human-centered AI systems [Graells-Garrido et al., 2025]. 

Moving beyond technical correctness, scholars have increasingly emphasized the usability of XAI as a key concern. Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research emphasizes that explanations must not only be accurate but also understandable and useful for decision-making [Picard et al., 2023, Reddy, 2024]. To this end, several studies have proposed design guidelines and evaluation frameworks for human-centered XAI, incorporating measures such as the System Usability Scale (SUS), Explanation Satisfaction Scale (ESS), and Trust in Automation (TiA) [Kong et al., 2024, Mohseni et al., 2018, Rong et al., 2022]. These metrics enable systematic evaluation of how explanations influence user confidence, understanding, and reliance on AI systems. 

In parallel with these efforts, no-code machine learning platforms have sought to democratize AI by allowing users to train and deploy models without programming. Platforms such as Google Cloud AutoML, H2O Driverless AI, Orange3, KNIME, and RapidMiner are increasingly used by business analysts, domain experts, and educators.

Title: The Role of Human Knowledge in Explainable AI
Snippet: Depending on their goals, background and relationship with the product, users are grouped in three categories: developers and AI researchers, domain experts and lay users. The author discusses the importance of approaching explainable AI in a user-centered manner, providing tailored explanations based on the needs and characteristics of the targeted group of users, finally improving affordability and user satisfaction, and easing the explanation evaluation process. Striving to understand how and why such groups employ explanations and behave, several researchers have carried out experiments by engaging specific user groups. Hohman et al. [95] involved professional data scientists to explore how and why they interpret ML models and how explanations can support answering interpretabilityrelated questions. More generally, users can be classified as domain or expert users and non-expert users. Nourani et al. [96] inspected the behaviour of such user groups on their first impression of an image classification model based on the correctness of its predictions. They discovered that providing early errors to domain experts decreases their trust, while early correct predictions help them in adjusting their trust based on their observations of the system performance. On the other hand, non-expert users relied too much on the predictions made by the model due to their lack of knowledge. Such over-reliance on the ML system [6,89,96] highlights how it is always necessary to account for the users engaged in the system. Moreover, while it is necessary to engage non-expert and end users in the evaluation of such system, it is also recommended to consider their features, preliminary knowledge and understanding of the system of interest. 

Finally, while explanations were proven to be effective in leading the user in achieving a task and improving their trust and understanding of the model, it has also been demonstrated that sometimes they are either not able to improve [97,98] or, worse, they reduce human accuracy and trust [99]. A similar result in a different context was found by Dinu et al. [100]. They focused on post hoc feature attribution explanations and discovered that such explanations provide marginal utility in our task for a human decision maker and, in certain cases, result in worse decisions due to cognitive and contextual confounders. Such findings bring forth a fundamental conclusion.
